title: Joshua 8:30–35
context: Joshua 8:30–35 records a covenant ceremony at Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim, carrying out Moses’ instructions in Deuteronomy 11:29 and 27:1–13. Joshua builds an altar of uncut stones, offers sacrifices, writes a copy of the law on stones, and reads the blessings and curses before all Israel, including women, children and foreigners. The unit stands as a whole and follows the battle for Ai. The Hebrew text places it here, while the ancient Greek translation places it after 9:2, so its position in the book has long been discussed. In either case its meaning is clear: after judgment and victory, Israel renews its commitment to the LORD’s covenant in the land he is giving them.

verses.text: Then Joshua built an altar to the LORD, the God of Israel, on Mount Ebal,
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua builds an altar “to the LORD, the God of Israel, on Mount Ebal.” After the campaign at Ai, Israel turns to worship. Arminian readers note that the people’s response to God’s grace is renewed devotion, and that worship and covenant commitment follow naturally from God’s deliverance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the altar stands on Ebal, the mountain of the curse (Deuteronomy 11:29), so sacrifice is offered where the curse is announced. Shared ground: both traditions read the altar as central to covenant renewal and see in the setting a pattern fulfilled in Christ, through whom God’s people are reconciled and enabled to worship.

verses.text: as Moses the servant of the LORD commanded the children of Israel, as it is written in the book of the law of Moses: an altar of uncut stones, on which no one had lifted up any iron. They offered burnt offerings on it to the LORD and sacrificed peace offerings.
verses.arminianNotes: The altar is built “as Moses the servant of the LORD commanded,” of “uncut stones, on which no one had lifted up any iron” (compare Deuteronomy 27:5–6 and Exodus 20:25). Arminian readers note Joshua’s careful obedience to the written law, and the burnt and peace offerings as expressions of dedication and fellowship with God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize that worship follows God’s revealed instructions, not human design, as the uncut stones show. Exodus 20:25 warns, “if you lift up your tool on it, you have polluted it.” Shared ground: both traditions read the burnt offerings and peace offerings as part of the Old Testament pattern of atonement and fellowship fulfilled in Christ.

verses.text: He wrote there on the stones a copy of Moses’ law, which he wrote in the presence of the children of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua writes “on the stones a copy of Moses’ law” in the presence of the children of Israel, following Deuteronomy 27:3, “You shall write on them all the words of this law.” Arminian readers note that the law is made public and accessible, so the people know what God requires and can respond to it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize the centrality of God’s written word in the life of his people. The law is set up in the land as the constitution of Israel’s life under God. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as honoring Scripture’s authority, and both see the public writing as calling the whole community to know and obey God’s word (compare 1:8).

verses.text: All Israel, with their elders, officers, and judges, stood on both sides of the ark before the Levitical priests, who carried the ark of the LORD’s covenant, the foreigner as well as the native; half of them in front of Mount Gerizim, and half of them in front of Mount Ebal, as Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded at the first, that they should bless the people of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: All Israel stands on both sides of the ark, half before Mount Gerizim and half before Mount Ebal, “the foreigner as well as the native.” Arminian readers note the inclusion of foreigners within the covenant assembly, a sign that God’s purposes reach beyond Israel’s ethnic boundaries, as Rahab’s story already showed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the ark, carried by the Levitical priests, stands at the center, signifying God’s presence at the heart of his covenant people. The arrangement follows Deuteronomy 11:29 and 27:12–13. Shared ground: both traditions see the inclusion of foreigners as an anticipation of the gospel’s reach to the nations, and both read the scene as a solemn renewal of covenant.

verses.text: Afterward he read all the words of the law, the blessing and the curse, according to all that is written in the book of the law.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua reads “all the words of the law, the blessing and the curse.” Arminian readers stress that the covenant sets before Israel real alternatives: blessing for faithfulness and curse for unfaithfulness. The people are called to choose obedience, as chapter 7 had shown the cost of disobedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that blessing and curse are both part of God’s covenant word, and both are read in full. The covenant’s sanctions are real, and the people hear them together. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a reminder that God’s word includes both promise and warning, and both see the curse ultimately borne by Christ for those who trust in him (Galatians 3:13).

verses.text: There was not a word of all that Moses commanded which Joshua didn’t read before all the assembly of Israel, with the women, the little ones, and the foreigners who were among them.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua reads every word of Moses’ commands “before all the assembly of Israel, with the women, the little ones, and the foreigners.” This fulfills the pattern of Deuteronomy 31:12. Arminian readers note that the whole community, including the most vulnerable and the outsider, is addressed as responsible to hear and respond.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize the completeness of the reading: “There was not a word” left out. God’s word is to be heard in full by all his people, from the youngest to the foreigner. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a model of public reading of Scripture and as showing God’s concern that every member of his people know his word.
